implementation_notes: From Java 9 the asynchronous default is a stage-level deadline: orTimeout(timeout, unit) completes a future exceptionally with java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException when it does not complete in time, completeOnTimeout substitutes a fallback value instead, and get(timeout, unit) bounds a synchronous wait on the same future. The class keeps at most one shared daemon thread for triggering delayed actions, so a deadline does not cost a thread per call, and the timeout completes the future without cancelling the work behind it.
pitfalls: orTimeout completes the future but does not cancel the underlying call: the HTTP request or RPC keeps running unless the client itself was given the budget.
join() throws CompletionException while get(timeout, unit) throws ExecutionException (or TimeoutException directly), so the same expiry needs different handling at different call sites.
An orTimeout stage keeps a delayed task registered until it completes; futures created per request must complete or be cancelled, or they accumulate on the shared delay scheduler.
completeOnTimeout turns a failure into a value, so callers cannot distinguish a fallback from a real result unless the fallback value is marked as such.

variants.name: ExecutorService + Future.get(timeout, unit) (classic blocking)
variants.implementation_notes: The classic realization submits the call to an ExecutorService and bounds the wait with Future.get(timeout, unit), which throws TimeoutException when the result is not available; the task itself keeps running and only cancel(true) (mayInterruptIfRunning) asks the executing thread to interrupt. It is the right shape when the surrounding code is blocking and thread-per-request, or when the call must run on a caller-supplied pool, and it costs a pool thread for the duration of the call - the very resource the timeout is meant to protect.
pitfalls: cancel(true) only interrupts: a task blocked in a non-interruptible syscall, or one that swallows InterruptedException, keeps running after the caller gave up.
get(timeout, unit) starts counting when get is called, not when the task was submitted, so time spent queueing before that call is unbounded unless admission is bounded too.
A shared executor saturates: enough blocked tasks starve every other caller, so the timeout has to be paired with a bounded queue and a rejection policy.
